questions.prompt: What does a single solid yellow line on a road mark?
choices: Lanes going the same direction on a one-way road.
The center of a road with two-way traffic.
The edge of a lane that is about to end.
questions.explanation: A single solid yellow line marks the center of a two-way road. Lanes going the same direction are separated by white lines.

questions.prompt: On a two-lane road, a solid yellow line runs on your side of the center. What does it tell you about passing?
choices: You may not pass the car ahead.
You may pass if no one is coming.
You may pass a car below the limit.
questions.explanation: With only one lane in your direction, do not pass when a solid yellow line is on your side of the road, even if the way looks clear.

questions.prompt: A broken yellow line runs next to your lane, with no solid line on your side. What does it mean?
choices: You may never pass on this stretch.
Only oncoming traffic may pass here.
You may pass, but only when it is safe.
questions.explanation: A broken yellow line next to your lane means passing is allowed when it is safe. Double solid yellow lines mean no passing.

questions.prompt: When may you turn left across a single set of double yellow lines?
choices: Never; they form a barrier you can't cross.
Only where there is a marked opening.
To enter a driveway or make a U-turn.
questions.explanation: You may turn left across one set of double yellow lines into or out of a driveway or private road, or to make a U-turn. Only two sets two feet apart form a barrier.

questions.prompt: Construction signs tell you to use the other side of the road because your side is closed. What should you do?
choices: Follow the signs, driving left of the double yellow lines.
Stay right of the double yellow lines and wait it out.
Turn around, since crossing double yellow is never allowed.
questions.explanation: When construction or other signs direct you to the other side because your side is closed, you may drive to the left of double yellow lines.

questions.prompt: Two sets of double yellow lines, two or more feet apart, separate you from a driveway on the left. May you turn left into it?
choices: Yes, since it is a private driveway.
Only at a marked opening in the lines.
Yes, after yielding to oncoming traffic.
questions.explanation: Two sets of double yellow lines two or more feet apart are a barrier. Don't drive over it or turn left across it except at a designated opening.

questions.prompt: Broken white lines separate the lanes on your road. What do they tell you?
choices: They mark the center of a two-way road.
Traffic in both lanes goes the same way.
You may not change lanes across them.
questions.explanation: Broken white lines separate lanes going in the same direction, and you may change lanes across them when safe. Yellow lines separate opposite directions.

questions.prompt: Double solid white lines separate your lane from a carpool lane. When may you move into it?
choices: Not until the lines change to a single broken line.
Whenever you have enough people in the car.
Whenever traffic is clear and you have signaled.
questions.explanation: Never change lanes over double solid white lines. Enter or exit an HOV lane only at its designated openings, where the line is single and broken.

questions.prompt: Your freeway lane is marked with large broken lines. What should you be ready for?
choices: The lane may exit the freeway or end.
A carpool lane is about to begin on the left.
Passing is now allowed on both sides.
questions.explanation: Large broken lines usually mark an ending lane. Be ready to exit or merge, and look for an exit or merge sign.

questions.prompt: What do white triangles like these across your lane show?

figure.alt: A row of white triangles painted across a lane, pointing toward the cars approaching it.

choices: That a speed bump is ahead.
Where to yield or stop.
Where a bike lane crosses.
questions.explanation: A yield line, a row of white triangles pointing toward you, shows where to yield or stop.

questions.prompt: On a freeway, which lane is the Number 1 Lane?
choices: The far-right lane.
The far-left, or fast, lane.
The lane nearest the on-ramp.
questions.explanation: The left (fast) lane is the Number 1 Lane; the lane to its right is Number 2, and so on.

questions.prompt: You are pulling away from the curb onto a street with several lanes. Which lane should you enter?
choices: The left lane.
The center lane.
The right lane.
questions.explanation: Use the right lane to enter or exit traffic or to pull out from a curb or shoulder. The left lane is for passing and left turns.

questions.prompt: Before changing lanes, you have signaled and checked your mirrors. What else should you do?
choices: Slow down to let the other lane pass you.
Look over your shoulder toward the new lane.
Change lanes; mirrors cover the lane beside you.
questions.explanation: Look over your shoulder in the direction you are moving to check your blind spot. You don't need to slow down to change lanes.

questions.prompt: On a dry road, there is a big enough gap in the next lane. How much must you slow down to change lanes?
choices: Not at all.
About 5 mph.
About 10 mph.
questions.explanation: If there is enough space in the next lane, you don't need to slow down to change lanes.

questions.prompt: Traffic is heavy on a multilane road. What is the safest way to drive?
choices: Switch to whichever lane is moving fastest.
Change lanes often to keep a steady speed.
Stay in one lane as much as you can.
questions.explanation: Weaving and last-minute lane changes raise the risk of a collision. Stay in one lane as much as possible.

questions.prompt: Halfway through a turn, you realize it is the wrong street. What should you do?
choices: Stop and back out of the turn.
Finish the turn and find another route.
Stop where you are and rethink.
questions.explanation: Once you start through an intersection or a turn, follow through. Correct your route later.

questions.prompt: You pass the street where you meant to turn. What should you do?
choices: Stop and back up to the corner you missed.
Keep going until you can turn around safely.
Turn right away, even from the wrong lane.
questions.explanation: If you miss a turn, keep driving until you can safely and legally turn around.

questions.prompt: How can you tell how many people you need to use an HOV lane?
choices: It is always at least three people, by law.
It is listed on your registration card.
Signs at the on-ramp or along the road.
questions.explanation: Signs at the on-ramp or along the road give the minimum number of people, and the hours HOV rules apply.

questions.prompt: May a motorcyclist riding alone use an HOV lane?
choices: No, only cars carrying passengers may.
Only with a special DMV decal.
Yes, unless a sign says otherwise.
questions.explanation: Motorcycles may use HOV lanes unless otherwise posted.

questions.prompt: How is the road surface of an HOV lane marked?
choices: With a diamond and the words Carpool Lane.
With green paint and a bicycle symbol.
With a row of white triangles.
questions.explanation: HOV lanes are marked with a diamond symbol and the words Carpool Lane.

questions.prompt: How is a center left turn lane marked on each side?
choices: A single solid yellow line on each side.
A broken inner line and a solid outer line.
Double solid yellow lines on both of its sides.
questions.explanation: A center left turn lane is bordered on each side by two lines: the inner one broken and the outer one solid.

questions.prompt: What may you use a center left turn lane for?
choices: To pass slow traffic when it is clear.
Only to start a left turn or a U-turn.
As a regular lane when traffic is heavy.
questions.explanation: A center left turn lane is only for preparing for and making left turns or U-turns. It is not a passing or travel lane.

questions.prompt: What is the farthest you may drive in a center left turn lane?
choices: 100 feet.
200 feet.
500 feet.
questions.explanation: You may drive no more than 200 feet in a center left turn lane, entering it within 200 feet of your turn.

questions.prompt: You are driving slowly on a two-lane road where passing is unsafe. What is the fewest vehicles behind you that requires you to use a turnout?
choices: Three.
Ten.
Five.
questions.explanation: If you are driving slowly and five or more vehicles are following, you must use a turnout area or lane to let them pass.

questions.prompt: When may you drive in a bicycle lane?
choices: To enter or leave the road.
To pass slower traffic on the right side.
Whenever no bicyclists are in sight ahead.
questions.explanation: Driving in a bike lane is illegal except to park where permitted, to enter or leave the road, or to turn within 200 feet of an intersection.

questions.prompt: How does a bike lane's line usually change near an intersection?
choices: The solid white line becomes dashed.
The solid white line becomes a double line.
The white line turns yellow.
questions.explanation: A bike lane's single solid white line typically turns into a dashed line near an intersection.

questions.prompt: What do chevrons or diagonal stripes beside a bike lane do?
choices: Mark a place to stop for loading.
Give more space from traffic and parked cars.
Mark an extra lane for turning cars.
questions.explanation: A buffered bike lane uses chevrons or diagonal markings to put more space between bicyclists, traffic and parked cars.

questions.prompt: You see a bicycle symbol with arrows painted in your traffic lane. What does it mean?
choices: Only bicycles may use this lane.
Bicycles must stay on the shoulder here.
Bicyclists may ride in the lane with you.
questions.explanation: Shared roadway markings tell drivers that bicyclists can occupy the lane and help bicyclists keep a safe position.

questions.prompt: What is a bike route?
choices: A lane on which only bicycles may ride.
A preferred route on streets shared with cars.
A path separated from cars by a curb.
questions.explanation: A bike route is marked with signs and shared road markings on streets shared with traffic. A path physically separated from cars is a separated bikeway.

questions.prompt: How far before a turn should you start signaling?
choices: About 100 feet.
About 50 feet.
About 25 feet.
questions.explanation: Start signaling about 100 feet before a right or left turn.

questions.prompt: As you turn right, where should you watch for bicyclists and pedestrians?
choices: Between your vehicle and the curb.
Only in the crosswalk ahead of you.
In the lane to your left.
questions.explanation: When turning right, watch for pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists between your vehicle and the curb.

questions.prompt: You have signaled for a turn at an intersection. What should you do as you approach it?
choices: Speed up so you clear the turn quickly.
Look over your shoulder and slow down.
Rely on your mirrors without turning your head.
questions.explanation: Look over your right shoulder and slow down before a right turn; for a left turn, look over your left shoulder.

questions.prompt: What is a limit line?
choices: A wide white line showing where to stop.
A yellow line marking where passing ends.
A row of white triangles where you yield.
questions.explanation: A limit line is a wide white line that shows where to stop before an intersection or crosswalk. White triangles are a yield line.

questions.prompt: There is no limit line, but there is a crosswalk. Where should you stop?
choices: On the crosswalk, short of the cross street.
Before the crosswalk.
Even with the STOP sign.
questions.explanation: Stop behind the limit line; if there isn't one, stop before the crosswalk; if there is no crosswalk, stop before the intersection.

questions.prompt: You stop at a limit line. Where should the front of your vehicle be?
choices: On top of the line.
Behind the line.
Just past the line.
questions.explanation: When stopping at a limit line, don't cross over it.

questions.prompt: Before turning at an intersection, in what order should you look?
choices: Left, right, then left again.
Right, left, then right again.
Left, then right.
questions.explanation: Look left, right, and left again before turning, and turn when it is safe.

questions.prompt: You are stopped at this signal. When may you turn right?
choices: After a full stop, if it is clear.
After the red arrow turns green.
After yielding to pedestrians.
questions.explanation: You may turn right on a solid red light after stopping, but not on a red arrow. Wait for green.

questions.prompt: You want to drop off a passenger, and the only free curb is along a bus-only lane. What should you do?
choices: Find somewhere else to stop.
Stop briefly with your hazards on.
Stop there if no bus is in sight.
questions.explanation: It is illegal to drive, stop, park or leave a vehicle in an area set aside for public transit buses, even briefly.

questions.prompt: When may you cross a bus-only lane?
choices: To pass slow traffic.
To pick up a passenger.
To make a right turn.
questions.explanation: You may cross a public transit bus lane to make a right turn, but you may not otherwise drive, stop or park in it.

questions.prompt: Your right turn lane doesn't merge into another lane and has no light or sign on its curb. Through traffic has a red light. What may you do?
choices: Stop fully first, as for any right turn on red.
Wait until the through traffic light turns green.
Turn without stopping.
questions.explanation: A dedicated right turn lane lets you turn without stopping even when through traffic has a red light, but you must obey any light or sign on its right curb.

questions.prompt: A left turn lane begins ahead, bordered by a solid line. When should you enter it?
choices: At its opening, without crossing the line.
As soon as there is room, crossing the line.
Only after your light has turned green.
questions.explanation: Enter a designated left turn lane at its opening, without crossing any solid line.

questions.prompt: You are waiting to turn left while oncoming traffic passes. Which way should your front wheels point?
choices: Straight ahead until you can turn.
To the left, ready to turn.
To the right, toward the curb.
questions.explanation: Keep your wheels straight while you wait. If they are turned left and you're hit from behind, you could be pushed into oncoming traffic.

questions.prompt: You turn left from a two-way street onto another two-way street. Which lane should you end in?
choices: The right lane nearest the curb.
The left lane nearest the middle.
Any lane that is open.
questions.explanation: Start in the left lane nearest the middle and end in the left lane nearest the middle of the street going your way.

questions.prompt: When may you turn left on a red light, after stopping?
choices: From one one-way street onto another.
From a two-way street onto a one-way street.
Never, under any condition.
questions.explanation: You may turn left on red from a one-way street onto a one-way street if no sign forbids it, after yielding to traffic and pedestrians with a green light.

questions.prompt: Which lane should you use to make a U-turn?
choices: The far-right lane, to swing wide.
The left turn lane or the far-left lane.
Any lane, once you have signaled.
questions.explanation: To make a U-turn, signal and use the left turn lane or the far-left lane.

questions.prompt: When may you make a U-turn in a residential district?
choices: Only at an intersection with a signal.
When no vehicles are coming within 200 feet.
When no vehicles are coming within 100 feet.
questions.explanation: In a residential district you may make a U-turn if no vehicles are approaching within 200 feet.

questions.prompt: May you make a U-turn at an intersection on a green light?
choices: No, U-turns at traffic signals are illegal.
Yes, unless a NO U-TURN sign is posted.
Only if you are in a residential district.
questions.explanation: You may make a U-turn at an intersection on a green light or green arrow unless a NO U-TURN sign is posted.

questions.prompt: How may you make a U-turn on a divided highway?
choices: Across the center strip, if it is flat.
Only through an opening in the center divider.
Across two sets of double yellow lines.
questions.explanation: On a divided highway, U-turn only where a divider opening is provided. Never cross a dividing section, curb, strip or two sets of double yellow lines.

questions.prompt: Where is it always illegal to make a U-turn?
choices: Across a double yellow line.
On a railroad crossing.
On a quiet residential street.
questions.explanation: Never make a U-turn at or on a railroad crossing. U-turns across a double yellow line, or in a residential district when no one is within 200 feet, can be legal.

questions.prompt: What is the least distance you must be able to see clearly in each direction before making a U-turn?
choices: 200 feet.
100 feet.
500 feet.
questions.explanation: Never make a U-turn if you can't see clearly for 200 feet in each direction.

questions.prompt: You need to turn around. Which of these is illegal?
choices: Using a fire station driveway.
Using a divider opening on a divided highway.
Making a U-turn at a green arrow.
questions.explanation: Never make a U-turn in front of a fire station or use its driveway to turn around.

questions.prompt: Where may you make a U-turn in a business district?
choices: Anywhere, if no one is within 200 feet.
Only in the middle of a block.
Only at an intersection or a divider opening.
questions.explanation: In a business district, U-turns are allowed only at intersections or at openings in a divided highway.

questions.prompt: When may you turn from, or into, more than one lane?
choices: When signs or arrows show you may.
Whenever the lanes are empty.
Only when on one-way streets.
questions.explanation: Signs or arrows show when you may turn from or end in more than one lane.

questions.prompt: You turn left from a two-way street onto a one-way street with three lanes. Which lane may you end in?
choices: Any open lane.
The far-left lane, as on any left turn.
The lane nearest the right curb.
questions.explanation: Start in the lane nearest the middle. If there are three or more lanes in your direction, you may end in any open lane.

questions.prompt: You turn left from a one-way street onto a two-way street. Where should you start and end?
choices: Far-right lane, then the nearest open lane.
Far-left lane, then any open lane you like.
Far-left lane, then the left lane nearest the middle.
questions.explanation: Start in the far-left lane and end in the left lane closest to the middle of the street going your direction.

questions.prompt: A bicyclist moves into the left turn lane ahead of you. Is this legal?
choices: No, they must cross as pedestrians.
Only if no cars are waiting in it.
Yes, bicyclists may use it to turn left.
questions.explanation: Bicyclists can legally use the left turn lane for their left turns.

questions.prompt: What is the smooth way to brake to a stop?
choices: Keep on the gas, then brake firmly at the end.
Ease off the gas, then press the brake lightly.
Press the brake hard, then let up and repeat.
questions.explanation: Take your foot off the accelerator, let the vehicle slow, then press the brake lightly, leaving enough space and time.

questions.prompt: You stop behind another vehicle. How much space should you leave?
choices: About one foot from its bumper.
Enough to see its rear wheels.
At least three car lengths.
questions.explanation: Leave enough space that you can see the rear wheels of the vehicle in front.

questions.prompt: When should you stop on a freeway on-ramp before merging?
choices: Only if it is absolutely necessary.
Always, to check for a gap.
Whenever a car is in the right lane.
questions.explanation: Merge when it is safe and don't stop unless absolutely necessary. Stopping makes it harder to reach the speed of traffic.

questions.prompt: On a freeway ramp, a solid line separates your lane from the next one. When may you cross it?
choices: Once the line ends or turns broken.
Once the next lane is clear.
Once you have signaled for five seconds.
questions.explanation: Don't cross solid lines when merging onto or exiting a highway. Wait until the line ends, however clear the lane or long your signal.

questions.prompt: You need to cross three lanes to reach your exit. How should you do it?
choices: All at once, while the lanes are clear.
One lane at a time, signaling each time.
Slow down in your lane until a gap opens.
questions.explanation: Signal and cross lanes one at a time, checking your blind spots each time.

questions.prompt: Signaling five seconds before a freeway exit covers about how much distance?
choices: About 100 feet.
About 400 feet.
About 1,000 feet.
questions.explanation: Five seconds of signaling before an exit is about 400 feet.

questions.prompt: To merge into traffic on a city street, about how big a gap do you need?
choices: About one car length.
About a full block.
About half a block.
questions.explanation: On city streets you need a gap of about half a block, around 150 feet. On the highway you need about a full block.

questions.prompt: To merge onto the highway, about how big a gap do you need?
choices: About a full block, or 300 feet.
About half a block, or 150 feet.
About two car lengths, or 30 feet.
questions.explanation: On the highway you need a gap of about a full block, about 300 feet. Half a block is enough on city streets.

questions.prompt: You are waiting to turn left. An oncoming car has its right signal on. What should you do?
choices: Turn now; it is about to turn right.
Wait until it actually starts to turn.
Flash your headlights, then turn.
questions.explanation: Don't assume an oncoming car with its right signal on will turn before reaching you. Wait until it starts its turn.

questions.prompt: To pass safely, what is the least distance a hill or curve ahead should be?
choices: 100 feet.
One-tenth of a mile.
One-third of a mile.
questions.explanation: A hill or curve should be at least one-third of a mile away before you pass.

questions.prompt: On a two-lane road you are nearing a curve and can't see around it. May you pass?
choices: No, not until you can see ahead.
No, unless the car ahead is very slow.
Yes, if you pass quickly.
questions.explanation: Don't pass near a hill or curve if you can't see whether traffic is coming, however slow the car ahead. It is especially dangerous on one- and two-lane roads.

questions.prompt: What is the closest to a bridge or railroad crossing you may pass another vehicle?
choices: 50 feet.
100 feet.
300 feet.
questions.explanation: Do not pass within 100 feet of an intersection, bridge, tunnel, railroad crossing or other hazardous area.

questions.prompt: Where should you not pass another vehicle?
choices: On a one-way street, on the right.
At crossroads and driveways.
On an open highway with two lanes your way.
questions.explanation: Don't pass at crossroads and driveways. Passing on the right is allowed on a one-way street or an open highway with two or more lanes your way.

questions.prompt: The driver ahead is signaling a left turn. How may you pass?
choices: On the right, if it is safe.
On the left, quickly.
On the right shoulder, if it is clear.
questions.explanation: You may pass on the right of a driver turning left when it is safe. Never pass on the left of a left-turning driver, or off the main road.

questions.prompt: A car behind you signals that it will pass you. What should you do?
choices: Speed up so it can't cut in.
Keep your lane position and speed.
Pull onto the shoulder to let it by.
questions.explanation: Let the vehicle pass, and keep your lane position and speed.

questions.prompt: To parallel park, what is the shortest space you should look for?
choices: Three feet longer than your car.
Exactly as long as your car.
Ten feet longer than your car.
questions.explanation: Look for a space at least three feet longer than your vehicle, and signal when you find one.

questions.prompt: After parallel parking, what is the farthest from the curb your car should be?
choices: 18 inches.
3 feet.
6 inches.
questions.explanation: You should end up parallel to and within 18 inches of the curb.

questions.prompt: You park headed downhill next to a curb. Which way should you turn your front wheels?
choices: Away from the curb.
Into the curb.
Straight ahead.
questions.explanation: Headed downhill, turn your front wheels into the curb so the car rolls into it, not into traffic.

questions.prompt: When you park on a hill, in which case do you turn your front wheels away from the curb or road edge?
choices: Headed downhill, next to a curb.
Headed uphill, next to a curb.
Headed uphill, with no curb.
questions.explanation: Only uphill with a curb do you turn the wheels away from it, letting the car roll back until a wheel touches the curb. Downhill, turn them into the curb; with no curb, turn them right, toward the edge.

questions.prompt: You park on a hill with no curb. Which way should you turn your front wheels?
choices: To the left, toward the center.
Straight ahead.
To the right, toward the edge.
questions.explanation: With no curb, uphill or downhill, turn the wheels right so the car would roll away from the center of the road.

questions.prompt: What does a white curb mean?
choices: Park for the limited time shown on a sign.
Load or unload freight for the posted time.
Stop only to pick up or drop off passengers.
questions.explanation: White curbs are for picking up or dropping off passengers only. Green is limited-time parking; yellow is loading.

questions.prompt: What may you do at a green curb?
choices: Stop only to pick up passengers.
Park for the limited time posted.
Park with no time limit.
questions.explanation: A green curb means limited-time parking, as posted on a sign or painted on the curb.

questions.prompt: You drive an ordinary passenger car. What may you do at a yellow curb?
choices: Park there for the whole day if you like.
Nothing at all; you may never stop there.
Load or unload, usually staying with your car.
questions.explanation: Yellow curbs are for loading and unloading passengers or freight for the posted time; noncommercial drivers usually must stay with the vehicle.

questions.prompt: What is usually the closest you may park to a crosswalk, marked or unmarked?
choices: 10 feet.
30 feet.
20 feet.
questions.explanation: Never park on a crosswalk or within 20 feet of one, marked or unmarked (15 feet where there is a curb extension).

questions.prompt: What is the closest you may park to a fire hydrant?
choices: 5 feet.
20 feet.
15 feet.
questions.explanation: Never park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant or a fire station driveway.

questions.prompt: What is the closest you may park to a sidewalk ramp for disabled persons?
choices: One foot.
Three feet.
15 feet.
questions.explanation: Never park within three feet of a sidewalk ramp for disabled persons, or in front of a curb that gives wheelchair access.

questions.prompt: Where is it illegal to park?
choices: At a green curb, within its time limit.
On a bridge where signs permit it.
Between a safety zone and the curb.
questions.explanation: Never park between a safety zone and the curb. Green curbs allow limited parking, and you may park on a bridge where signs allow it.

questions.prompt: You need to run into a shop for a minute, and no parking spaces are free. What should you do?
choices: Keep looking for a legal space.
Stop in a red zone with your hazards on.
Double park if a passenger stays in.
questions.explanation: Never park or leave your vehicle double parked, even for a minute, with the engine running or someone inside.

questions.prompt: When may you park in a space marked for zero-emission vehicles?
choices: When no other spaces are open nearby.
For up to 15 minutes in any vehicle.
Only if you are driving such a vehicle.
questions.explanation: Never park in a space for parking or fueling zero-emission vehicles unless you are driving one.

questions.prompt: When may you park on a bridge?
choices: Only where signs permit it.
Anywhere you leave room to pass.
Never, even if signs allow it.
questions.explanation: Never park in a tunnel or on a bridge unless signs permit it.

questions.prompt: Which of these ways of parking is illegal?
choices: With two wheels up on the sidewalk.
Twelve inches out from the curb.
Twenty feet from a fire hydrant.
questions.explanation: Never park on a sidewalk or partly blocking one. Parking within 18 inches of the curb, and more than 15 feet from a hydrant, is legal.

questions.prompt: Your car breaks down on the freeway. What should you do?
choices: Park fully off the pavement and stay inside.
Stop in the right lane with hazards flashing.
Walk to the nearest exit to get help.
questions.explanation: If you must stop on a freeway, park completely off the pavement and stay in your vehicle with the doors locked until help arrives.

questions.prompt: What is the shortest time a vehicle may be left standing on a freeway before it may be removed?
choices: One hour.
Four hours.
24 hours.
questions.explanation: A vehicle stopped, parked or left on a freeway for more than four hours may be removed.

questions.prompt: Which habit helps you use less fuel?
choices: Speeding up and slowing down smoothly.
Keeping your tires a little underinflated.
Carrying extra weight for better traction.
questions.explanation: Smooth, steady driving, properly inflated tires and less weight in the vehicle all improve fuel efficiency.

questions.prompt: An officer signals you to pull over. How should you show that you have seen them?
choices: Turn on your hazard lights and stop.
Turn on your right turn signal.
Wave out of your window.
questions.explanation: Turn on your right turn signal to show the officer you see them, then pull over safely.

questions.prompt: You are in the carpool lane when an officer signals you to pull over. Where should you stop?
choices: On the left shoulder, beside the carpool lane.
On the right shoulder.
In the carpool lane itself.
questions.explanation: Move completely onto the right shoulder, even from the carpool lane, and stop in a well-lit area if possible.

questions.prompt: After pulling over for an officer, what should you do?
choices: Stay in the car unless told to get out.
Get out and walk back to the officer.
Get out and wait beside your car.
questions.explanation: Stay inside your vehicle unless the officer directs you to get out.

questions.prompt: As the officer walks up to your car, where should your hands be?
choices: In clear view, such as on the wheel.
Reaching for your papers in the glove box.
In your lap, below the window.
questions.explanation: The driver and all passengers should place their hands in clear view before the officer makes contact.

questions.prompt: When must an officer tell you the reason for a traffic stop?
choices: Before questioning, except in an imminent threat.
Only if you ask, once they have your license.
When the stop ends, as they write the ticket.
questions.explanation: Officers must state the reason before questioning you, unless withholding it is needed to protect life or property from an imminent threat.

questions.prompt: When stopped by police, what must the driver show?
choices: Your driver's license, nothing more.
License, insurance, and registration.
Your license and your vehicle's title.
questions.explanation: A stopped driver must produce a driver's license, proof of insurance and vehicle registration.

questions.prompt: You don't produce your license, insurance, and registration when stopped. What may officers do?
choices: Nothing, until you find them yourself.
Do a limited search for them.
Impound your vehicle at once.
questions.explanation: If a driver doesn't produce these documents, officers may conduct a limited search for them.

questions.prompt: During a traffic stop, an officer tells your passenger to get out. Must they?
choices: No, only the driver must.
Only if the officer gives a reason.
Yes, they must comply.
questions.explanation: An officer can legally require the driver and all passengers to exit or stay in the vehicle, and you must comply.

questions.prompt: During a traffic stop in California, who may ask about your immigration status?
choices: Only federal officers.
Any officer who stops you.
Local police, but not state officers.
questions.explanation: Only federal law enforcement can ask about immigration status. State and local officers may not ask, and you can decline to answer.

questions.prompt: You are recording a traffic stop without interfering. Which is true about your phone?
choices: The officer can't take it for that alone.
The officer may delete what you recorded.
The officer may take it if you keep recording.
questions.explanation: If your recording doesn't interfere with the officer's duties, the officer can't confiscate your device, delete the recording or destroy the device just because you're recording.

questions.prompt: You want to record a stop, but your phone is in the glove box. What should you do?
choices: Reach for it quickly before the officer arrives.
Get out and record from beside the car.
Ask before reaching for it.
questions.explanation: Don't reach into concealed areas for your recording device without permission.

questions.prompt: You believe an officer is violating your rights. What should you do?
choices: Object out loud, but don't resist.
Physically block the officer.
Drive away and report it later.
questions.explanation: Even if you think your rights are being violated, don't physically resist or use violence. You may voice your objection.
